Question: Why isn't English a Latin language?
Answer: Your grasp of the migratory history of Britain is a little tenuous. The Romans came. They stayed for a few hundred years (quite a lot of them weren’t actually Roman, but let it pass). They went away again (Well, most of them. Some had intermarried with local girls, and probably stayed, but most of them went). By about 407AD they had gone. Some of the Britons they left behind might have picked up a bit of Latin, but I doubt if they used it much once the Romans had gone and there was no-one to talk Latin to. Then the Saxons arrived, and the Angles, and the Friesians, and the Jutes, from Germany, Friesland, Jutland or assorted other places just across the North Sea. Being basically German, they spoke a form (well, several forms) of German. And having come, and finding no Romans to be difficult about it, they stayed. Their Germanic language drifted away from its roots a bit (rather like American English having drifted away from the English English of a few hundred years ago) and developed into what is now called Old English, but which people used to call Anglo-Saxon. And that stuck, pretty well, until about 1100, 1200 even. There had been Vikings along the way (they spoke what we now call Old Norse, but it was a sort of harsh cousin of Old English, so they could understand each other) and then in 1066 the Norman French arrived. They were basically of Viking stock too, but their ancestors had gone the long way round and settled in France, so they now spoke a form of French - which was descended from Latin, as you know. And as they won the Battle at Senlac (confusingly known as the Battle of Hastings) and were now in control, French became officially the language of government. But still, there were only a few thousand Normans at Senlac, and many times that number of Saxon descendants spread all over the country as a whole. So although Latin genes now crept into the language, it took a very long time for them to get well established. And there were always a lot more Saxon (and Viking, and Celtic) genes in the system than Norman French ones. It took several hundred years for the two languages to merge properly. It only starts to look a bit like a recognisable, blended language by about the time of Geoffrey Chaucer, in the late 1390s. So there you are. That’s why English isn’t a Latin language - because most of its ancestors weren’t Roman. Edit: I thought (hoped) I’d explained this clearly enough, but have just had someone saying (in effect), “But what’s the difference, it’s still just from Latin, isn’t it, like French?” So here, just to show it a different way, is the prettiest language family tree I have ever seen: English Language Family Tree You’ll notice that both the Romance branch (which includes all the Latin-based languages) and the Germanic branch start off from the European branch. You can get more detailed views of some of the main branches here: A language family tree - in pictures . So English is mainly descended from the same set of ancestors as German. But because it has spent time with, and has married into the same family as, French, it has picked up some French and Latin characteristics that show through, even though they’re not the main ancestral line. Does that help? I do hope so.

Question: Everyone in my life is discouraging me from trying to do medicine because of my gcse grades. I got 8777777755. Will my grades prevent me from doing medicine?
Answer: Well, those are perfectly respectable GCSE results in themselves. But they don't suggest a student who is statistically likely to get excellent A level results, and that's the part that makes it unlikely that you'll get a place at university to do Medicine. It's a heavily oversubscribed subject, and even people expected to get 3 A*s don't necessarily get in. At this moment, there's no indication that you'd be likely to get grades like those - Bs and Cs are far more likely. But still, that's just statistical probability, not Predicted Grades. Now you have a year in which to turn the chances around, by working really hard and becoming the sort of excellent student who gets the right kind of grades. As long as the two 5s weren't for science subjects, then enrol to do A level Chemistry (definitely), Biology (or maybe Physics) and perhaps Maths (definitely, if you do A level Physics), and really work at them. Also, get a voluntary part-time role in a local care home or hospital, or join the St John Ambulance Brigade, and stick at it; real commitment is what Admissions teams want to see, as well as the grades. If, in a year's time, you look like a good prospect for Medicine, then go for it. But if Medicine is slightly out of reach, there will be plenty of other things you could do instead, including things like Biomedical Science. So there's nothing to lose, and everything to gain. I hope it works out for you.

Question: In the UK, why exactly would someone with autism be entitled to extra time in their exams for A-level?

The detailed report from the clinical psychologist assessed her as being well into the 90th+ percentile on almost everything, but only the 4th percentile on processing speed. She pointed out that she had to check absolutely everything, to be sure that it was right. This approach certainly cost her at least one job, in an administrative role, where there was a strong target culture, and hitting your daily quota of completed tasks was more important than their accuracy. She works at the speed she does, very well, but not fast. Her thought processes are lightning fast, but that's no help in exams, especially as she's slightly dyspraxic, and writes very well but slowly. So clearly she would always be at a disadvantage in timed exams, despite the very high standard of her responses. I don't think she ever had extra time in exams, in fact. But you can see, I hope, why it might have been both appropriate and fair.

Question: I was predicted an A* in IGCSE Lit in English (0475), but ended up getting the lowest grade in my class on results day, obviously shocking everyone. Is it therefore advisable to appeal for a remark?
Answer: Not necessarily. Examiners aren't usually fools, and if you got a low grade, there will have been reasons for this. But just in case… You can ask for a photocopy of your exam scripts. This will enable your teachers to look at them, and see if they broadly agree with the marking, or if they think it's wildly out. And if they think the marking is totally wrong, that's the time to request a re-mark. Students sometimes do very strange things in exams. Not really answering the question asked is the commonest problem; you can write reams of really good stuff that doesn't earn you any marks at all, because it just doesn't match up with the mark scheme. But equally, there have been cases of examiners missing entire double pages of a script, or their checkers failing to add up the allocated marks correctly, so their overall total is wrong. So ask your school to request a photocopy, and get your teachers to check your part of it. And if everyone thinks it's strange, then go for a remark.

Question: How do you write an essay about a thief that stole a car and when he sees the police road block ahead his heart beats fast?
Answer: You don't. That's not an essay, in which you discuss something, or argue a point of view. That's a story, in which you imagine what happened, describe it, invite your reader to feel part of the action. Imagine you're there, and you're the thief. How are you feeling? What do you do? What happens? How does it all end? That's what you write about! The only alternative, if it really is an essay that's required, is that this is in response to a question on Human Biology, in which you are required to write about the physiological responses to the stressful situation, of what this does to his heart rate and pulse, his breathing, to his body's production of adrenaline, and its effects, and so on. But it has to be either this or the story.

Question: Growing up how common were working mothers among your peers?
Answer: In the late 1950s and early 1960s, in the UK? I didn't know anyone whose Mum went out to work. By the late 1960s, one of my friends had a mum who was a history teacher, but she is literally the only one I can think of. Most of them hadn't worked outside the home since they got married; they'd have felt they weren't doing the job of being a wife properly, and that it implied that their husband couldn't provide for his wife and family. Ten years later, by the late 1970s, it was normal for young women like my friends and me to work full-time until we had our first baby, perhaps returning to work once our children were all at school, though preferably only part-time, by which time we're well into the 1980s. And after another ten years, it was becoming normal for women to be back at work full-time once their maternity leave was over, but then taking another batch of maternity leave for second and any other babies. And these days, a great many women stop after just one baby, because childcare is too expensive. Sad, isn't it?

Question: Can you get into Oxford University if you don't have good grades and have barely done any extracurriculars, but will start doing better? I'm in 11th grade by the way.

She came to the UK from a school in Hanoi for gifted students, and she turned out to be not just brilliant and hardworking, but a delightful person too. She was a top student in Maths, French, Photography and Textiles, and she went to the University of the Arts, London to study Fashion Design. She's doing very well professionally, combining Business and her creative skills. She was quite bright enough for a top university like Oxford, but it wouldn't have been what she needed at all. So forget fantasies of Oxford. Start really working, build a portfolio of good artwork, and apply for the right kind of courses at the right sort of universities or colleges. Just not Oxford or anywhere like it.

Question: When will Oxford call me for an interview? Can anyone who applied in Oxford get the call?

Still, on the assumption that you will be able to, then when might such a call happen? Try this webpage: And there you will find that, as interviews generally happen in the first few weeks of December, the invitations happen in the second half of November, sometimes giving barely a week's warning. There's lots of other information on that part of Oxford’s website. Read it, search it, and get into the habit of looking things up for yourself. Because, no matter what university you eventually go to, you will need to become an active learner, rather than someone who sits and waits to be told things. It's probably not the way you've been used to learning up to now, but if you want to go to university in the UK, or anywhere else in the Anglosphere, it's the way you will in the future. And the time to start is now.

Question: A student gets A*A*A*A* at A-level, an A* in her EPQ, and a 1st-class mark in a 15-credit level-4 module. Would you encourage her to consider re-applying to the University of Oxford even if she says that she is happy to go somewhere else?

She's clearly an outstanding student, and it's perhaps surprising that she didn't get into Oxford. Question: How do I decide my A-level subjects? I am a private student so I do not have access to career counselling. I am unsure what to pursue in my further studies.

The ideal result is to find yourself doing, for money, what you would do anyway for the pleasure of it.

Question: So I got a 67%, which is a C grade in my AS level. Is it possible to turn this into an A grade during A2?
Answer: No, it isn't, unless you retake the AS modules and do much, much better. Your overall grade will be the average of the two parts AS and A2. And it's not possible to achieve an average of A unless the lower grade is at least a B. Not only that, but because A2 is built on the work you did in AS, and is much harder and more demanding, most people go down by a grade between AS and A2. This means that statistically you are more likely to get a D than a B, let alone an A. So if you are going to beat the statistical odds, you are going to have to work incredibly hard. You need to start by revising all your AS work, and start that now. You need to be aiming for A grade work ALL the time, and constantly practising and checking. The ball is in your court.

Question: How would you recommend to spend a gap year if you are reapplying to university so as not to feel bored or depressed?
Answer: First and foremost, I would recommend doing something that's new to you, having new experiences that will extend your life in new directions, expand your horizons, and build your confidence in your ability to cope with the world. What form this takes will depend entirely on you, on where you are (physically, mentally and socially) and what's normal for you. For me, having been a boarder at school for 7 years, what I most wanted was a time of living at home, and getting a job in the local town. But it quickly transpired that this really didn't fit with my father (I think he'd got rather used to having the house to himself, and a lifestyle that didn't include a resident daughter), so he pushed me into a residential course in cookery and housecraft, things that hadn't been part of my school education. I went, with massive reluctance, endured it for half a term, and then got myself a residential job, working in a children's home in Bristol. It was a totally new experience, introducing me to a completely new world of other lifestyles, and gave me both freedom of movement in a new city (bookshops and cafés!) and an income, which also meant the freedom to do things like going off and spending weekends with a friend, without having to ask anyone if I could, or indeed even telling anyone. It was a wonderful taste of independent life, and very instructive. It built my confidence in things like travelling independently, and in my ability to cope with new situations, even in small things like being happy to cook for a dozen people, whilst on a university field trip. Not the most glamorous way to spend a half-gap-year, but I've never regretted it. These days, people go for much more organised and ambitious gap years. The daughter of a friend started off with a paid-for half year in Thailand, then went for the second half to New Zealand, where the paid-for arrangement fell to bits. So she found a cheap backpackers’ hostel, scrubbed floors to afford it, then found a sailing job on a tall ship, and spent the next few months cruising on board the ship, visiting interesting places, painting murals on board the ship, and cooking for the crew. She had such a good time that she took a second gap year, working as a chalet maid in Switzerland, improving her skiing and learning snowboarding, then teaching skiing and snowboarding in Chile. Her third gap year involved more teaching winter sports, and running an art gallery, in Canada, then helping with developing a surfing resort in Peru. She won an award for that. She then went to university, three years late!! She now runs her own company, a seaweed business in Cornwall. She's a totally surprising person. So gap years can be whatever you make them. For you, Maudlina, I think getting more used to being in new places, and coping with everyday things like getting independently from one unfamiliar place to another, might be a priority, but as long as it's something that expands your ability to cope with life and the unexpected, it will probably be good. The best of luck with the coming year! I hope your A level results were as good as you hoped, and that your university applications take you in a good direction, whether that turns out to be Cambridge, Oxford or somewhere else. 😊

Question: My son gave A level exams at different times in three subjects. He wants a single certificate of A level result. Is it possible?

Question: What should I do? Should I take a gap year to retake my GCSE (as I have got straight C grade in science subjects) before starting A-Levels, or begin A-Levels now and retake O-Levels after? I'm aiming for a medical university in Pakistan on merit.

Question: Are ACC as level results okay? I need an A*BB to get into the uni I want, however, I get 2 grade reductions from my pathway. I’m on track to get an A* in my math.

So saying that you need A*BB is only possible once you have received a Conditional Offer and have accepted it. You can't have, at this stage. Still, let's suppose those are the grades you will need. Firstly, you need to start working really hard. Your Edits log suggests that school or college work hasn't been exactly your main priority this last year, and it's going to need to be. And secondly, you need to retake those AS modules, and get them up to As, not Cs, so that even if you get only Cs for them at A2 level, you'll have Bs overall. Because if you don't, you won't get the grades you need. Better get offline, and start revising last year's work - right now!

Question: If colleges only care about A-levels, then what's the point of I/GCSEs?
Answer: Colleges, American style, have their own system and criteria. But universities, UK style, care about both. Your GCSEs or IGCSEs are important mainly as an indicator of how well you are likely to do at A level. Really good results at that stage say you'll almost certainly do well at A level, and mediocre ones predict far more ordinary results at A level. It's the overall pattern that matters, not just results in the subjects you're going to take at A level. Oh, and really bad results suggest that academic work probably isn't your thing, and you'd do well to forget university. If you don't want to go to university anyway, then why take A levels? If you have already got your A level results when you apply to university, then the GCSEs/IGCSEs are much less important. But they do still matter, as representing the pattern of your secondary school education and achievement, so nobody is saying you don't need to worry about taking them seriously. Does that help?

Question: Will the income from part-time jobs be sufficient for living and paying university fees in the UK?
Answer: Not a chance! Living and paying tuition fees in the UK will cost you around £30,000 per year, possibly much more. This means that you would need a pre-tax income of at least £40,000 per year, which is considerably more than most young university graduates earn, working full-time. There is no way you will be earning that sort of money in a part-time job delivering pizzas or working at the local supermarket (typical student jobs). In any case, you will be restricted to a maximum of 20 hours per week of working during term time. This is normal in most countries. Try to exceed that, and you're likely to get your visa revoked, and you will be deported. If you do try it, and start missing lectures or work deadlines as a result, your university has to report this, which makes it extremely likely that you will be caught. Besides, you have to pay your fees upfront, at the start of the year. And to get a visa at all, you'll need to demonstrate to the UKVI that you've got enough money in the bank to cover your whole expenses for the entire first year, and to assure them that you do not need to work in order to afford it. Once again, get caught lying to them and you can expect your visa to be revoked, and yourself deported. Coming to the UK to study is very expensive. Unless you really can afford it, I would strongly recommend that you stay at home!

Question: What should I do to get into Oxford for engineering as a high school student?

Question: Why has my wife struggled with the IELTS reading module, failing it seven times despite multiple attempts?
Answer: She hasn't failed it. Nobody ‘fails’ IELTS tests, because there isn't a Pass/Fail border. It's designed to be a measure of how good your English skills are, that's all. As to why your wife's Reading skills aren't as good as you think they should be, how can we possibly know? How much English teaching has she had from teachers who are native speakers of English? How much opportunity does she get to practise reading in English, and particularly reading the kind of texts that might come up in the exam? Do you encourage her to read things online like articles in The Guardian or on the BBC News website? Does she read English books? All of these are things that would help her to improve her reading skills, because practice is important. But does she actually want to, anyway? There's an old saying: you can take a horse to water, but you can't make it drink. And if your wife isn't interested in reading, and doesn't want to, then she's most unlikely to improve. Have you tried asking her about this?

Question: How far back into your childhood can your remember and what is your favorite memory of that time?
Answer: My very earliest memory appears to date from about the time of my first birthday. It's very clear, and can't possibly have been implanted in my mind by anyone else, because no-one else was there or would know about it. And it's definitely not a dream, but a clear memory. It's daytime, summer, and although the curtains on the window are closed, from the light around them and filtering through them, I can see that the sun is shining outside. It's my bedroom, and I'm in my bed, which must be a baby's cot. Outside my bedroom, the other side of the wall behind my head, I can hear footsteps coming up the wooden stairs. I know those footsteps, and they belong to the doctor. I don't like the doctor, because every time he comes, he makes them cover me with that horrible pink stuff with the horrible smell, and I feel I can't breathe. There is nowhere I can go, so I burrow under my bedclothes. That is all. My only clue to the time or the circumstances came from my mother, who died before I was 10. She mentioned once that I had measles just about the time of my first birthday, and that she'd always thought I caught measles from the doctor, because I hadn't been anywhere else where I could have done so. Well, my birthday is in August. The curtains would have been closed to protect my eyes, if I had measles. And the horrible pink stuff would have been calamine lotion, a kaolin-based remedy intended to soothe itchy spots. 70 years on, I still hate the smell of it! We left that beautiful cottage two years later, and I miss it to this day. I remember the kitchen, with its scrubbed wooden table and its red-tiled floor, and the Aga cooking range that kept it warm all year round; my father had bought it from an old house, and rebuilt it in our kitchen. I discovered recently that it's still there, nearly 70 years after we left, and so are the tiles. Both must be well over 100 years old. Someone rightly commented below that the scrubbed table and tiled floor would have made a lot of work, but we did have a cleaning lady, a Mrs Trevor. The reason why I remember the kitchen table is because I also have a memory of Mrs Trevor being on her hands and knees, scrubbing the floor, having parked me on the table to keep me out of the way and out of mischief. I must be a toddler, and I'm sitting, as toddlers do, with my legs outstretched in front of me, feeling the ribbed surface of the scrubbed table on the back of my legs. In one hand I have a small chunk of lemon, in the other a little salt, and I'm alternately licking the salt and sucking the lemon. Below me, Mrs Trevor (whose hair is tied up in a headscarf) is looking up, and telling me what a peculiar child I am! I remember our sitting room, the green-covered armchairs and the black and white television with the tiny screen. I remember our garden, and the scary geese at the bottom of the garden; I remember the muddy lane outside and the surrounding fields. I loved every inch of it. I would go back in a heartbeat!

Question: When should I ask someone if they’re gay?
Answer: Mostly, I don’t think you should, unless it’s obviously relevant. Most of the time it won’t be. How often do you find you need to ask people you don’t think are gay about their patterns of sexual activity or choices of sexual partner? I would suggest, hardly ever. I think I’ve only ever asked someone this question once in my life, and only then because it was necessary. I had a bright, intelligent and hardworking student in my Tutor Group, a really lovely young man, who was obviously very unhappy, suddenly telling me about the terrible confrontation with his mother that weekend, in which he’d had to tell her that the person he wanted to spend the rest of his life with wasn’t the person she’d always assumed. As the person he was always with in college was an exceptionally pretty girl, bright, intelligent and lovely, absolutely his equal, and they always looked incredibly married, I could guess who his mother was thinking of. So I asked him, “Forgive me for asking this, but are you saying that you told her you’re gay?”, because I had to be sure I'd understood him correctly. And he said simply, “Yes.” We then had a very calm, sensible conversation about his mother’s shocked reaction, and about mums and their love for their children, and how I wouldn’t have guessed either, so I could see why it came as a shock to her. I assured him of my conviction that Mum would be fine once she’d got over the shock, and that she would go on being as proud of her very impressive son as she always had been. And so it turned out. When his mum and her partner got married soon afterwards, he was actually Best Man at the wedding, and his partner was a guest. They were all fine. And he completed his A levels, got very good results, and went on to university as scheduled. He and his partner married, are still together, and are doing fine. So I did ask him directly, because it was necessary. But mostly it isn’t necessary or relevant, so unless it obviously is, then mind your own business. What other people do in bed, and with whom, is usually nothing to do with the rest of us.

Question: If I want to get all grade 9s in my GCSEs, should I be revising in the summer after year 10?
Answer: Well, yes, some, but then, ideally you should have been doing a bit each week, ever since the start of Year 10. Likewise, a bit each week during Year 11 - and you can probably guess what I think you ought to do during Years 12 and 13. A bit each week, just looking back over the week's work, will help to fix it in your mind with no great effort. It also gives you the chance to go back and ask your teachers about anything you don't understand, missed or otherwise can't resolve. Then a half-term recap, and again at the end of each term, and the same at the end of the year. Second year, same as the first. But a little bit harder, and a little bit worse! Seriously, if you follow this kind of pattern, by the end of the course you will know all your work very well indeed. Now of course this is a counsel of perfection, a “don't do as I did, do as I say!” bit of advice. But maybe, if someone had said this to me 60 years ago, my exam results would have been quite consistently good, instead of being excellent in the things I loved, and a bit bleah in the things I didn't. I had the pleasure of a rare meeting with my cousin's son yesterday. He's American, 18, a really interesting person, and very definitely a smart kid. He accused himself of being lazy, and I said this was actually very normal for people like him; they're so used to everything being easy, that the hardest thing for them is learning how to work. I had the same problem, and perhaps you do too, OP. But if you follow the advice I've given you, then provided you can match work with ability, you should be on track for good grades all round. Success to you!

Question: If I fail maths GSCE, can I resit in November and change my A levels if I pass?

However, I don't think you'll be able to change subjects at that point, because you'll have missed a whole term's work on any new subject, in fact about half the year's work, since the Autumn term is so long. Catching up would be huge. And in any case, I don't think doing any subject like Maths or Physics at A level sounds like a good idea for you. You need to be confidently expecting a 7 in GCSE Maths at least, probably an 8, or even a 9, to be planning on A level Maths, and a minimum of a 6 for anything like Physics or Economics. A scraped 4 or 5 just won't do. It really doesn't sound as if Maths is a strong subject for you. I hope you do pass first time, but I do seriously think you should give a lot of thought to your A level choices, between now and the end of August. Best of luck!

Question: What's the average age of first time mothers?
Answer: It's impossible to answer this truthfully and simply, because it depends on the part of the world where you live, and changes over time. When I had my first baby, I was 28, and the medical profession in the UK classed me as an “elderly primigravida,” ie old for a first-time mum. Two other ladies gave birth the same evening; both were a farmer's wife, both were 40, and both had a baby boy. One was having a fourth attempt at producing a son for her husband to leave the farm to, but for the other it was a first baby. The nursing staff thought having babies at their age was quite amazing. Those babies are all now in their 40s. Now, 28 is no longer considered “elderly” for having first babies, and first babies at 40+ are no longer unusual. And it has its points. For many years it's been said that the ideal time for giving birth is when you're about 17. However, the best age for bringing up babies and children was said to be in your 40s. It seemed that the answer was for young daughters to produce the babies, and then let Mum and Dad bring them up, while the young couple lived, worked, and earned the necessary money to pay for things. But now that so many women of 40 are having babies, Mum and Dad can do the babysitting in their 60s!

Question: How can I get the IELTS degree in English?
Answer: It's not a degree! IELTS stands for International English Language Testing System, and is a standardised way of testing your skills in Speaking, Listening, Reading and Writing in English, to provide an overall picture of your skills in English. Most people who take it need it for a visa to allow them to work or study in an English-speaking country. You can take the tests in almost every country in the world, but it's quite expensive, and it's probably not a good idea to take it until you are fairly sure you are ready. I would suggest that you find a good teacher of English as a Foreign Language, and get some help from them. It will cost some money, but it will be cheaper than taking the test many times!

Question: If I take 1 Cambridge and 2 edXcel A levels exams, do most universities accept that as a total of three subjects, since I think Cambridge math suits me more?

Question: Why have conservative supporters taken the 2024 July election result so badly?
Answer: Have they? What is your evidence for this claim? Footage of Conservative voters rioting in the the streets, perhaps? Or news film of them marching on Parliament, trying to break in, claiming that the whole General Election was a complete fake, Labour are trying to steal the Election, and Rishi Sunak is still Prime Minister really? I pause for a reply…. Or maybe there isn't one, because absolutely none of this happened - this being the UK, you understand? Because I'm sorry to disappoint you, but we really don't do this sort of thing here. I'm usually a Conservative voter, have been since 1970, in fact, and this was really not the result I'd have wanted. But as sure as night follows day, and for similar reasons, I knew it was the way we were going. I knew it as soon as Conservative Party members (of which I'm not one) elected Liz Truss as Party Leader. I even said so on here, at the time, as someone reminded me about an hour ago. But even without Liz Truss, it was almost certainly going to happen. Whichever party is in government inevitably gets farther and farther out of touch with the general public, and becomes arrogantly convinced that they know best, even though they're basically a bunch of amateurs in the job, at best; worse still are the professional politicians who've never done anything else, and know absolutely zero about life in Education, Health, Defence, Business or Engineering, but don't let that get in their way. The longer they are in, the worse they get. And sooner or later, the general public becomes so fed up with the whole boiling lot of them that they chuck them out, to give the other lot a go. How much worse can they be? The trouble is that the longer a government is in, the more voters there are who have no memory at all of anything else. So naturally, when (for example) Labour tells the public that the only reason things are not all lovely is because the Wicked Tories just want everyone to be miserable, and are refusing to let us have nice things, these innocents are likely to believe them. If only Labour were in, they tell us, everything would be wonderful. And it doesn't matter how many oldies, like me, have seen all this, heard it and lived through it, several times before, nor how many times we try to tell them that it never, ever works. The starry-eyed innocents who haven't are not going to believe us until they've experienced it all for themselves. And then, a few years down the line, having lost patience, they'll vote them out and let someone else have a go. It was bound to happen. We knew it was. And in any case, we knew that Rishi’s lot were making a complete mess of the job - they'd long passed their Best By date, and needed chucking out. It doesn't mean we have any great hopes of the new lot - but that's a very long way from “taking it badly.”

Question: What are the differences between my English teacher would wear colour socks, coloured socks, and colourful socks?

Question: Did your parents ever say you were an accident? How did you respond?

Question: I am fancy to learn old fashioned descriptive British English in formal terms, but how can I find it on the internet?
Answer: English changes all the time. The English we speak now would sound unrecognisable to someone who spoke the English of a thousand years ago, and very strange to someone of Shakespeare’s time, about 400 years ago! English of a thousand years ago is a foreign language to us, and nobody speaks it any longer. It's called Old English. There are people who can read it and understand it, but not many. The language of Shakespeare, or of the Bible and Book of Common Prayer published in the early 1600s, is easier, because although people don't talk or write like that now, many of us have read them and can understand it quite easily. And besides, it's more modern, more like modern English; it's called Early Modern English, and you can find all of Shakespeare and the King James Bible online. But please don't try to write like that, or even in the style of Jane Austen (who died about 200 years ago) or Charles Dickens, who was living and writing after Jane. She didn't write elaborate descriptions, but he did, and although some of his are wonderful, the style is not something anyone would want now. Nobody has time for such lengthy sentences at such a slow pace! Let me put it like this, and you can see what I mean about not using the styles of the past: For verily, thou shouldst eschew the fashions of ancient times. Thou shouldst not write in this wise, neither shouldst thou speak so unto thy neighbour. Were it otherwise, surely would I counsel thee to employ so great a style, but lo, in these times men would esteem thee passing strange, and an alien from a foreign land. For no man speaketh thus unto his neighbour, nor unto even the alien within his gates. Speak our speech, I beseech thee, in the manner of our land, and not of the ancients! Or, to put it another way: Please don't try to write or speak the way people did hundreds of years ago! People will think it's very strange, because nobody talks like that now. Learn good modern English, and use that instead.

Quite apart from anything else, her airframe was reaching the point of being no longer airworthy. Metals reach a point of no return, and simply come to the end of their life. You can't go on using a craft with metal fatigue. Besides, these aircraft from years ago were serviced regularly and kept in good condition by highly-experienced and very well trained aircraft mechanics, who knew and loved those engines and airframes. My husband spent 10 years in the Fleet Air Arm, 8 of them as a Naval Air Mechanic, back in the 1960s, and there was very little he didn't know about the McDonnell Douglas Phantom or the Blackburn Buccaneer. Many of the more robustly rude exchanges then, which everyone took for granted, and accepted without turning a hair, would now get you dismissed the Service, and probably pilloried in the Press too. Being PC wasn't even in their vocabulary, still less in their psyche. So you've got to start off with their Political Re-education, and I don't think they're going to like it, let alone reform willingly. It's going to be a long process, and that's just before you let them anywhere near the young mechanics of today. World War III will probably be over by the time you're trying to get those Buccs, Harriers and Tornadoes airborne. I think Tom Lehrer (another non-PC leftover) had it right. There isn't going to be much time! By the way, I should also have mentioned the slight problem of spares. Our son works for a company that makes parts for the aircraft industry, mostly programming machines to turn a billet of metal into a complex part, in one single process, in long production runs. Question: Is it true that real reason for more than 7 million people waiting for treatment with UK’s NHS healthcare system are its doctors treating private non-NHS patients and allocating 2 weekdays to working on personal things?
Answer: No, it's not as simple as that, and your question is mixing up two entirely different sets of doctors. The problem most people have with getting an appointment to “see their doctor,” ie a GP (General Practitioner) at the local practice, involves almost entirely doctors who work with the NHS. There's a major shortage of them at present, for a variety of reasons I'll look at below, and that's where the big holdup is. They are not specialists who can just decide to work privately some or all of the time; private GP practices are few and far between. Why are we short of GPs? A variety of reasons, but for many of them the work has become increasingly stressful and the workload intolerable, and although earlier generations of GPs were willing to work themselves into an early grave in the process, their younger colleagues are increasingly inclined to say, “No, I won't! I'll work fewer hours and accept the reduction in my earnings, but I'm not a slave, and I have obligations to my family and myself.” So they do, and they can't be compelled to do more than they are willing to do. Push them too hard, and they might just give up altogether, or emigrate, as many already have. So train more doctors, then! Well, yes, but the number they can train is limited by the number of available placement spaces. Then, it takes about 7 years to grow some new doctors, and they won't all choose to be GPs anyway. But the wastage is quite high; quite a number opt out before they're fully trained, or within a very short time after qualifying. And then there's the awkward problem of gender. For reasons of equality, they try now to train as many women as men, which is fine; many women make excellent doctors. But bright, healthy and therefore attractive young women (because being young, fit, intelligent and healthy is inherently attractive) tend to attract partners, and therefore to get married and to have babies quite soon, and that means maternity leave. Even when the maternity leave ends, there's a fair chance that they'll decide to go part-time rather than full-time on their return to work. So the unfortunate truth is that training 10 new young medical students, which is very expensive, for 5 - 7 years, isn't going to get you anything like 10 new, full-time GPs. I suspect that the true figure is probably nearer to 3 FTE (full-time equivalent) doctors. It could be even less than that. The other part of your question, the accusation that doctors are wickedly treating private patients at least some of the time, is a bit of a red herring. For a start, this means senior doctors in hospitals, the Consultants, who do have this option, not the GPs, and whilst it's true that they can and do, much of the private work involves NHS patients anyway. I've had two knee replacement operations done, both in a local private hospital, as an NHS patient, and the surgeon who conducted both operations does both private and NHS work. He does some of his NHS work in the big general hospital across the road, and some at the small private hospital. He's still treating patients though, however they're funded. I was sent to the private hospital by the NHS because I was in otherwise good health, and looked like a very straightforward case. This freed up bed space in the general hospital for someone less well than I was, but with the same need for orthopaedic surgery. This is standard practice, and it's hard to see how it disadvantages anyone. So to sum up, the TL, DR answer: There's a considerable queue at present because there is a shortage of FTE doctors, and you can't just wave a magic wand and produce more doctors. And you can't force people to work more than they are willing and able to work, because if you try, you'll lose even more of them, and make things worse rather than better.

Question: If I want to enter the undergraduate program at Oxford, do I have to exceed the requirements of the university (for A level/IB)? Do universities treat those who meet the requirements equally?
Answer: Well, firstly, there's no such thing as “the undergraduate program” at Oxford, or indeed any UK university except possibly the Open University. You apply to study a particular subject, and the entry requirements will vary from subject to subject. If you are seriously interested in applying to Oxford, you really should have researched this already for yourself, rather than making vague assumptions and asking for the information; you couldn't possibly survive Oxford like this, and probably not even get in. Still, since you asked: you choose your degree subject, and go to either UCAS or Oxford’s website to find out their minimum, and typical, entry requirements. If you and your teachers think that you are likely to achieve those grades, then you go ahead and apply online, via UCAS (their website being Choose your future ), no later than the 15th October (the deadline is always the same), and ask your teachers to supply your Predicted Grades and a Reference. For some subjects, there are also assignments or tests set by Oxford as their own assessment of your eligibility. There is nothing automatic about your being accepted, even if your grades do look good enough; there's a fair way to go, yet. After that, you wait, and hope. If they think you look like a possible candidate, they will invite you for interview, usually around November, and this is the real test. You will have at least two very challenging interviews, for which all you can do by way of preparation is perhaps a practice interview or two, and get used to thinking for yourself. Because that is what will be needed in your interview; you will be faced with unexpected questions, and expected to think about them and respond intelligently. There's no question of learning things beforehand, so don't try. They're far more interested in your level of intelligent interest and ability to think on your feet, than in your subject knowledge. And then you go home and wait again. And some time around mid-January, you will find out whether or not you have been successful! I notice that someone else says that British students have a built-in advantage. Personally, I think they should have (it's a British university, after all), but in practice it seems that they don't; all the statistical evidence confirms this. So go for it. What is there to lose?

Answer: We don't have to do anything of the kind. They're suggestions, at most. Being advised to start your question with a question word, such as Who, What, When, Where or Why, is intended to help, but it's not a rule, not an order. And the same applies to A2As, or Requests to Answer: you can answer if you wish (as I am at present), but you don't have to. It isn't a job, we're not being paid, and you're free to enjoy it!

Question: Can I complete studying IGCSEs 6 subjects in 9 months without any prior reading? Also, is CS too hard? Should I take it?
Answer: Possibly - but without knowing you, it's impossible to say. In theory, it's doable, if you've got the ability, the motivation, the determination and the resources. Way back in about 1970, when my future husband was a sailor in the Royal Navy, his Divisional Officer informed him that he was far too troublesome on the lower deck (ie, as a common sailor), that he was to go to Dartmouth (the Navy's College for trainee officers) instead, and that for that he'd got six months to get 5 O levels, whilst also working full-time. When the Navy tells you to do something, it's an order, so you do it! And he did. Later on, those five O levels, coupled with having been an officer in the RN, also helped to get him into university. So yes, it can be done. But whether or not you can do it, I can't possibly predict. That's all down to you!

Question: Are Muslim immigrants becoming well enough integrated into the UK?
Answer: For the most part, they tend not to want to assimilate, and work very hard at maintaining absolute separateness. In the road where I live, there are about 50 houses, semi-detached or detached houses built between two world wars - nothing grand, but basically quite houses, in good repair, with central heating, double glazing, garages, driveways and gardens. Some are let to groups of students (we're very close to the University), but most are owner-occupied. And I think between 10% and 15% are occupied by Muslim households. They're all very pleasant. They'll chat as you go past, and one couple actually has a small dog, a small white poodle, which they take past our house when they're out for walks; they always smile and say hello. Another neighbour (a first-generation immigrant) is a widower with three grown-up children, all of whom did well at school and went to university. The oldest and youngest are a solicitor and an accountant; I'm not sure what the middle one is doing now. The second daughter is still single and is living independently in London, but her elder sister (the solicitor) had an arranged marriage, to a cousin from Pakistan, and has recently had their third baby, another girl, which everyone seems happy about. They're all living in the same house, though actually it's no longer the one in this road, because they've recently bought a bigger house round the corner, to accommodate them all. I think they're planning to sell the old one. I've had cups of tea in their old house, and must go and visit them in the new one. Cousins of theirs live a few doors away from us. The father in particular is very nice; his father was the immigrant, so he was born and brought up here, went to the best school in the city and to university here; he's an accountant. He's cheerful, friendly and easy to chat with; if all Muslims in the UK were like him, nobody would have any problems with Muslim immigration, but unfortunately they aren't. Like his uncle down the road, he's got three grown-up, university-educated children, and now a baby granddaughter, as well as two cats. I know the baby and her parents live a short distance away, in the most expensive district of the city, which is now almost exclusively Asian-owned, but the daughter often brings the baby over here in her little car, and I see her father (my nice neighbour) proudly carrying his little granddaughter, in her baby car seat, into the house. I've been inside their house (which is very nice, modern and extremely comfortable) just once, when I was one of two non-Muslim neighbours invited to a party before the son's arranged wedding, and we both felt very honoured to be invited. This was some years ago, though, and as far as I know, the bride is still in Pakistan. So those are the three Muslim families I know best in this area. They're all pleasant and at least outwardly friendly, and are very acceptable neighbours. They're mostly well-educated and in professional occupations, but except for possibly the daughter who has escaped to live in London on her own, I don't think any of them are what you would call integrated or assimilated. They live distinctively culturally-separate lives, and even the babies attend the local mosque on Fridays, at least until they start school. They're here, it's home, but only up to a point. I don't think you could criticise this or call it unreasonable. Their cultural and religious background is Pakistani Muslim, not a European Christian tradition, and you can't expect them to change from that, or not in less than a good many generations. They're keen to maintain their traditions, or at least many of those traditions, which is understandable. But I think this is top-end Muslim integration. In many other cities, particularly in the North of England, there are large areas where almost everyone is Pakistani Muslim, fairly poor and Urdu-speaking, and where many of them are barely aware that they are part of only a small percentage of the UK population. Surveys there have indicated that many of them are under the impression that England is about 90% Muslim, whereas it's actually well under 10%. But it's not surprising; if you live in an area of a strange country where everyone you see looks like you, and speaks your language, then it must seem likely to you that everyone else in this unfamiliar country does, too. It doesn't even occur to them to think that they need to integrate - why, and with what? Some of them must probably wonder why they're here - it's just like home, only with less-good weather! So that's where we are so far. It'll probably change with time, but how much time? I have absolutely no idea.

Question: Do you expect free refills (at least of the sandwiches and possibly also scones) as standard as part of afternoon tea (i.e. the traditional British meal often served in hotels)?

Question: Why does the Oxford Advanced Learner's dictionary not say that the word "doctor" can mean "to cure"? It's used in this meaning in "The Hobbit": "The dwarves revived him, and doctored his scorches as well as they could". Other examples can be found.
Answer: That doesn't mean that they “cured him” as in “made him completely well again,” which is how it's normally used. Strictly, “cured” really means cared for, took care of; we see it in religious terminology, with words like “The cure of souls” and “curate.” So they didn't manage to leave him perfectly healed. They doctored him, looked after him as well as they could, but that doesn't imply pristine perfection. So why doesn't the dictionary say it means “to cure,” with that sense of cure? Partly because it doesn't, I think. And the very best dictionaries don't really give you exact synonyms anyway. They'll give you examples of the word in use, and close approximations - but not exact synonyms, because really, there aren't any. The real skill in English is in judging, accurately and sensitively, exactly which word, out of several words of very similar meaning is the one that most precisely conveys what you are trying to say. It's about being able to recognise its mood, message, and connotations, and understand how other readers in English are likely to receive it. And becoming a really good writer is all about being able to do that successfully. I'm not brilliant at it, but I'm slowly improving - after only 70 years!

Question: I have an IGCSE score of 10 A*. I have an IB predicted score of 43. Is it enough to study material science in Oxford?

Unlike you, apparently, I've just checked, which took me a few seconds, and the answer was here: But GCSEs, IGCSEs, A levels and IBs are only the basic requirements. Your interview is your opportunity to persuade them that you would be the sort of person they'd enjoy having in their College, and to be teaching - and for you to get an idea of whether or not Oxford would suit you (in my case, we both decided it probably wouldn't, and I've always been glad I didn't go there, but it might suit you). Oxford has very short teaching terms, only 8 weeks long, but very intense. And a huge amount of effort and initiative on the part of the student is needed, as well as a lot of independent work done in your own time - it's not like a more advanced version of school. You need to be an enterprising and active learner, someone who goes looking for answers, and not just someone who works diligently under direction. Possibly you are, but this question doesn't sound like it. Quite possibly you live (I haven't checked) in a country where that just isn't the way teaching and learning are done, but it is here, increasingly as you get towards university. So if Oxford really is what you want (and remember that plenty of other good universities are also available), then you need to start developing your skills of independent learning. Good luck. I hope this is helpful.

Question: Why is Quora making strange questions that I answer into my questions? They are making it look like I said things about placentas and brothers insults.

And you've been here two months at most!), Elizabeth Funchess, I think I know what's going on. You write thousands of extremely brief answers, often less than a single line long, to a huge range of questions, some of them the sort of weird questions that most of us would ignore, Pass on or Downvote. Unfortunately, the Quora algorithm concludes that you like this sort of stuff, and shows you ever more of it. Engage with such questions, and get sent more of them - that's how it works. And because Quora takes the view that all Questions on here belong to the whole Quora community, any Question you engage with instantly becomes, in Quora's language, “your question.” That doesn't mean that you wrote it, but just by responding to it, you've made it yours. So the answer is simple: don't! Why are you doing it, anyway? Answers as brief as those are unlikely to be good answers. Nobody wants to read them, and nobody is going to pay for them. It's entirely up to you, and you're entitled to do it, but I really can't imagine what you get out of writing them. 13,000! Question: Can you recommend hymns for Christians?
Answer: Well, I think that three of the greatest of the lot are “And Can it Be,” “To God be the glory, great things he hath done,” and “Thine be the glory, risen, conquering Son,” but there are plenty of other good ones, some much newer than others. “The Servant King” is excellent, for instance, and almost anything by Stuart Townend; “In Christ Alone,” or “How Deep the Father's Love For Us” are just two of his. John Bell, of the Iona Community, writes lovely contemporary hymns, often with Scottish melodies, and striking social relevance to our times. Isaac Watts, born here in Southampton 350 years ago next weekend, wrote hundreds of hymns, many of them still well-known today, and the best-known of the lot, “O God, Our Help in Ages Past” is played hourly by the chimes of the Civic Centre clock. The Wesleys wrote a great many that are still in very regular use, too. Someone else has mentioned “Dear Lord and Father of Mankind,” which has not only excellent words but a really beautiful tune, and the same is true of “My Song is Love Unknown,” and a wonderful Welsh hymn that I know in English as “Here is Love, Vast as the Ocean.” I've only once heard it sung in Welsh, on a Sunday evening round a piano, in a pub on Anglesey a few years ago, and it was just beautiful. There are hundreds, thousands to choose from. What are you looking for?

Question: When you block and mute someone on Quora, how can s/he still respond to your questions?
Answer: They can still answer your questions. Anyone on Quora can answer any question, because you don’t own the questions you ask - they belong to the whole Quora community as soon as you’ve asked them. You do own your answers, so you can stop people from commenting on them, by blocking them, or from sharing your answers or messaging you. If you’ve muted them, Quora won’t show you their questions in your feed. But if other people whom you follow answer their questions, or share their answers, then you may well see them. That’s how blocking and muting work. The next time you set out to block someone, before you confirm it, actually read what effect Quora tells you it will have, and I think you’ll find I’m right. After all, that’s the only reason why I know!

Question: How is a TV programme conveyed from the studio, videotape or film to the transmitter? Was it done the same way as now when TV first started? How are programmes conveyed to relay transmitters? How is regional programming in a network coordinated?
Answer: Once upon a time, it was all recorded on film, which began changing to videotape in the late 1950s. By the early 1970s, in the UK, this was the norm. In those days, quite a high percentage of the BBC output was actually transmitted live, rather than being prerecorded, which is how famous incidents such as the visit of a baby elephant to Blue Peter in 1969 could happen on air. Why did no-one realise what could go wrong?? News, chat shows like Parkinson, plusTomorrow's World, Tonight and a whole host of others were all broadcast live, however risky. Blue Peter and Tomorrow's World were both broadcast live (from the biggest studio at the Television Centre in Shepherd's Bush) on Thursdays, and the time interval for cleaning up (e.g after unexpected elephant-related incidents) after Blue Peter, and preparing the set-up for Tomorrow's World and experiments that might or might not work, was quite short. Guests on live chat shows like Parkinson might not behave quite according to plan, as Mohammed Ali and Rod Hull's Emu demonstrated: Similarly, when Tom Lehrer was a late-night guest on Parkinson in October 1980, he was able to launch straight into singing “I Got It From Agnes” on air, at a time when all his records in the BBC vaults were still marked “Not to be played on air without permission,” and get away with it. Because space was limited, and videotapes took up space, companies like the BBC routinely overtaped material they didn't expect to need again. The BBC in particular is notorious for being a poor judge of public taste, and having zero sense of humour, so it overtaped, and therefore lost, quite a lot of material still remembered by the public with enormous affection, and which would have had considerable commercial value for resale. Now, of course, in a digital world, this is less of a problem, as storing programmes takes up almost infinitely less space. Transmission in the UK was via a number of masts at stations like Droitwich, as with radio. But anything from abroad had to be via underwater cables, long before the invention of fibre optic cable, before the introduction of communications satellites such as Sputnik in 1956 began to transform the world. So TV material from America began to be transmitted to the UK by Telstar in 1962, and the footage covering Kennedy’s assassination, in November 1963, was memorably clear. Before 1962, I can remember seeing grey, fuzzy something on television, which my mother assured me was coming all the way from America, and it might as well be coming from the bottom of the Atlantic; there were moving, grey forms that might be human, and it was impossible to make out more than that. By the time we were receiving the first television footage from the Moon, in 1969, it was fractionally clearer than that early footage from America, about ten years earlier. This is not a technical response to your question, Charles Stuart, but is based on a combination of memories, including memories of a guided visit to the BBC Television Centre in the late 1970s. I hope it's a useful supplement to the more-technical answers you will probably receive from other people. And you might find the timeline here of interest and use!

Question: In the novel Pride and Prejudice, by Jane Austen, why is Lady Catherine de Bourgh styled 'the Right Honourable', a style borne by privy counsellors and by peers beneath the rank of marquess?

Question: Are immigrants included in population statistics? For example, does Britain have 67 million British citizens or are immigrants also included in this figure?
Answer: They are definitely included. Question: How come in East Asian cultures dead bodies are more likely to be cremeated than put in graves to decay?
Answer: Sheer practicality, I think, as the initial motivation, but over a long period of time, practical considerations get coated with tradition too. And two major factors will be speed and space. Bodies start to decay quite quickly after death, and the warmer the climate, the faster decay sets in. Rotting flesh attracts flies, which lay eggs, which turn into maggots - it's not going to be pretty, and the smell is going to be awful, if you don't either refrigerate or otherwise dispose of the body, and fast. Refrigeration is pretty new. In the UK, along with other European countries, few people had an ordinary fridge in the kitchen before about 1960, just about 65 years ago, though they were fairly common in America earlier than that. And most countries in Africa and Asia still didn't have them for many years after Europe did, in fact many people in those countries still don't. What would be the point, anyway, if you don't have electricity to power such things? So refrigeration in morgues and undertakers’ premises were also not widespread. Arranging burials takes time, including finding somewhere suitable to bury the person who has died, and digging a hole deep enough and long enough. Cremation is fast, and the resulting ashes take up much less space than a coffin. A funerary urn of ashes can be buried, or the ashes scattered, but sometimes people just keep the ashes with them. Space is a major consideration, and in the UK at least, cremations are far more usual now than burials. I'm 71, and I can think of only 3 burials I've attended that were of bodies rather than ashes after cremations. As populations grow (and the world's population has quadrupled in my lifetime) available space shrinks, and full graveyards become a problem. So it's not just hot countries in Africa and Asia where cremations are usual - Catholic countries in Europe probably still prefer traditional burial, but in Protestant and secular countries (and the UK is both of these), even cooler ones, cremations make sense. Possibly America is the exception, rather than the norm? I'm just guessing, but if you are American, OP, and it's not the norm where you live, then remember that the rest of the world has reasons for doing things differently!

Question: Is it Irresponsible of me to spend 14k out of my 50k savings in order to take a 35 day solo Euro trip, renew my wardrobe, learn scuba diving, and buy myself an omega watch and? I'm 19 years old and I have a full ride scholarship in a premium uni.
Answer: Well, if you can't be irresponsible for a month at 19, when can you? I don't know how anyone of your age manages to have 50,000 dollars, pounds or whatever in savings, and how you manage to have arranged a full scholarship too, when money is clearly not a problem, is a mystery to me, but in your enviable situation I'd go for it, or at least most of it. 35 days, or 5 weeks, is not long enough to do more than a whistle-stop dash around Europe; I think perhaps you're American, and the 14K is 14,000$. I've lived in the little UK almost all my life, and not seen all of it; my husband and I once spent 3 months in France, Italy and Malta, and barely scratched the surface of any of them. Malta and its little sister islands Gozo and Comino are very small, and a month there wasn't nearly enough; there was a lot we didn't have time to see. And that's just a little group of islands off Sicily, which is the triangular ball at the toe of the boot of Italy! Even Sicily is much bigger than you think. So I wouldn't try to do all of Europe; it will become an exhausting blur, of which you'll remember almost nothing. 35 days is less than a day per country, and half of it will be wasted in airports. I'd recommend slowing down a bit, and doing things that will fill your mind with wonderful memories, to stay with you. Avoid the big, classic tourist attractions: they're all full of tourists, most of them American, and you'll hardly be able to see the places, the things, for people. Someone I know lives on Gozo, where he is an underwater photographer; his wife is a diving instructor. They've just had several days of a Japanese visitor staying with them, learning both photography and scuba diving, and she's clearly had a wonderful time. Just 9 days, and she'll remember it for the rest of her life, as well as enjoying her two new skills. There is an important difference between being a traveller and a tourist. Tourists essentially get passively taken places and shown things, whereas travellers go places, do things, see and experience things. Your plan starts off by sounding like travel, but as soon as you start wanting to visit X countries in Y days, you've become a tourist. It will be expensive, and basically forgettable. Be a traveller; take charge, do things you never normally would, and accrue experiences and memories. Fifty years ago, my then-fiancé and I spent a week sailing on Loch Ness, and then another week camping in the Scottish Highlands. The weather was wet and miserable, and the midges never let up for a second, but it was great. For two nights we shared our campfire, and a bottle of memorably wonderful malt whisky, with an American guy who was cycling around Scotland, and camping. I wouldn't mind betting he still remembers that vacation today. Similarly, a few years ago, on a narrowboat holiday on the Trent & Mersey Canal, we met a young American couple from Silicon Valley (Google and Apple), doing the same thing as their honeymoon! They had wanted to do something no-one they knew would have done, and this was it. They were having a glorious time, operating locks, donking along at about 3 miles per hour (yup, that's correct - though the official speed limit is 4 mph!), enjoying the countryside and meeting people, and were planning to come back next year and do it again, on a different canal. And I'm willing to bet it wasn't costing them anything remotely like 14,000$, even though they probably could have afforded it. It's not a race. Do something active, and store up memories and experiences. And forget the Omega watch!

Question: Why is "s" in "dose" pronounced /s/, although in "rose" it's pronounced /z/, and why is "s" in "rinse" pronounced /s/, although "s" in "cleanse" is pronounced /z/? Is there any logic?
Answer: They just are! Look, it's no good expecting spoken English to follow rules, just because of the way words are written. It doesn't work like that. Americans in particular (not all of them, but a significant minority) tend to think that spoken English ought to be obedient to rules of spelling, and do as the written language tells it, and this is putting the cart in front of the horse! All written English is just an attempt to represent on paper, or on screen, what people say. And sometimes it doesn't do this very well. Ever since the days of Dr Samuel Johnson in the 18th century, and his great English Dictionary, spelling in the UK has been fairly fixed, and the Oxford English Dictionary rather compounded old Sam's work. It sets down spellings very firmly, tells you about the etymology and origin of each word, and tells you how to pronounce it. But pronunciation doesn't always stay fixed, and in the UK particularly, we have a huge number of local accents to contend with as well. Not only that but different dialects, including that American one. So I speak very standard English, as most of my family does, though my brother and his wife have more Midlands accents than I do, and their son, my nephew, sounds distinctly Australian, having spent most of his 22 years in New South Wales. My grandson, however, aged 9 and never lived outside Southampton, has been exposed to so much American influence on screen that he insists the number between 19 and 21 is “twenny.” And because he lives too near to a small town known to its residents as “beas'ly Eas’leigh,” he calls the wet stuff that comes out of taps “wau’a.” He'll still write “water” and “twenty,” though, because he knows how to spell them. That's just how it is. Please don't worry about it! An afterthought: Someone is bound to wonder, “Well, if that's so, why keep standardised spelling? Why not update it to match what people say? Why can't we go back to spelling things the way we like, instead of having to follow rules?” Well, whose English are we going to match it to, and when? The result is likely to be chaotic. And very difficult to read! You don't think so? Then have a look at this, an extract from the extraordinary novel Riddley Walker, written by the altogether amazing Russell Hoban. Riddley Walker lives in Kent, in England, but quite a long way into the future. There has obviously been a major war, and he and his people are scratching an existence in a desolate landscape, mostly by digging up metal materials to use or sell. And schools and literacy have clearly been casualties of the times and conflict, so Riddley can only tell his story by trying to represent the way he talks. The whole book is written like this. You'll get the hang of it, if you persevere long enough…

Question: I know someone who says his paternal grandfather died in world war 1 and his maternal grandfather died in world war 2. How can this be?
Answer: It's perfectly possible. I'm 71. My paternal grandfather was born in about 1884, and served in the Indian Army and in the Hampshire Regiment. He was gassed in the trenches of Northern France in World War I. As it happens, he survived, and lived until 1961, but he could easily have died during that War. His three elder children were born in 1910, 1912 and 1915, so it would not have precluded his having grandchildren if he had died then. My maternal grandfather was younger, having been born in 1902. He managed to serve in the Royal Navy during WWI, despite this, by adding a few years to his age, and joined in 1917. He must have married in about 1920, and he and my grandmother had two children, born in 1922 and 1924. By the time World War II began he was working for an aircraft manufacturer, Boulton Paul, who built the Defiant, so even if he hadn't been around 40 by then, his occupation would have meant that he would not be called up. The factory where he worked was a few miles outside Wolverhampton, and only one bomb ever fell anywhere near it. But had he been working instead for Supermarine in Southampton, building Spitfires, it might have been a very different story. The factory at Woolston was repeatedly bombed, and in one raid in the autumn of 1940, over 100 workers were killed. He could very easily have been one of them. His son and daughter would have been just 18 and 16 by then. So yes, the situation your friend describes is perfectly possible.

Question: Do those who are skilled at cooking at home (not professionals who cook en masse) prefer gas, electrical units, or induction method?
Answer: I'm interested in the answers singing the praises of induction hobs; this is something I've never tried, but they do sound good. However, as several people have said, we all tend to like what we're used to, and I certainly like the arrangement we have. This consists of a gas hob, and a separate electric oven. The oven is actually two ovens in one; it's a fan-assisted oven, which heats up and cooks faster than a conventional one, has consistent temperature in all of it, rather than being hotter at the top and lower at the bottom, and doesn't need to be as hot as a conventional oven. It has a very gentle defrost setting, which I use mostly for allowing bread to rise, and it's self-cleaning. But it's also a conventional oven. I realised this only when, on one occasion, I was preparing to bake some bread, and the fan in the back failed, so that the oven wasn't heating up. So I turned the dial, found the conventional oven setting, and discovered that that was working. I set the temperature rather higher than I usually do, and baked the bread as normal, just for slightly longer. It worked fine, and we replaced the fan unit next day. So I like my electric oven. But above it is a gas hob, and that was definitely a matter of choice. It has 5 burners, of 4 different sizes; the big one in the middle has a double ring of gas jets, and is perfect for doing things like stir frying, being very hot. Gas offers instant temperature control, which is why I always choose it; conventional electric cookers are better now than they used to be, but always used to take a long time to heat up and cool down. If that's what you have, you learn to use it effectively, but I like a flame I can see, and instant control. It also means that if, for any reason, the electricity supply fails, there's still an alternative means of cooking. I like the dual fuel option; to me, it's the best of both worlds. Gas hobs and electric ovens are a common combination in the UK, which is why I'm surprised that no-one else has so far mentioned them. Maybe it's just that not everywhere has a piped gas supply?

But still, it's rare in the UK, if not quite as rare as it used to be. So every time someone is stabbed and killed, in the UK it's major, and is headline news - not just in the UK but around the world. If such events aren't headline news when they happen in your country, then that's because they aren't so unusual as they are in the United Kingdom.

Question: If a female actress is required to smoke cigarettes for a movie and she doesn't know she's pregnant and has a miscarriage, who is the person to be blamed for it?
Answer: That's extremely hypothetical, and really not at all realistic. Yes, smoking while pregnant is not a good idea. It reduces the level of oxygen to the foetus. So if the pregnancy did terminate prematurely, it would be extremely difficult to prove that smoking a few cigarettes for the film was to blame, and the studio would undoubtedly fight the case, with a very good chance of winning. Remember: correlation is not proof of cause and effect!

Question: Why is the Tory party now so unpopular? Have the British people really forgotten the mess created by New Labour?
Answer: Yes, of course they have. It's 14 years since we last had a Labour Prime Minister, so people aged 18 now, and just eligible to vote, were only 4 then. Nobody of 30 or less will really have any clear memories of a Labour government, and so it's easy for lots of people to swallow the line that “If only we had a Labour government, everything would be lovely - the only reason it isn't now, is because of the Wicked Tories, who just want us to suffer!” We were in just the same situation in 1997, when Tony Blair was elected - and in 1964 when Harold Wilson was. I'm 71, so I can remember all of this clearly. I was still only 11 when Wilson first became Prime Minister, so I was too young to have known anything about Clement Attlee's government, but I do recall the Labour mantra of “13 years of Tory misrule!” It happens again and again. Labour promises the earth, promises everything will be lovely, gets in and spends money like water. The economy falls to bits, and the country sighs, holds its nose and elects the Conservatives to tidy up the mess. Sometimes this can be an extremely painful process; after Margaret Thatcher’s stint in the job, most of us prayed we'd never need to go through all that again. It was horrible, but after Wilson and Callaghan, long, miserable years of endless strikes and rampant inflation, it was necessary. But once the suffering was tailing off, there was a collective sigh of relief, and the country turned to Labour again, with its promises that everything would be lovely now. Tony Blair was actually not too bad, if you set aside things like the Iraq war, largely because he actually admired Margaret Thatcher and copied much of her approach, but things went badly downhill once Gordon Brown took over. Sadly, we haven't had a really good Prime Minister since Margaret Thatcher and Tony Blair, of either colour. The other thing that happens, regardless of which lot is in power, is that after a couple of Parliamentary terms they become complacent, and start to develop an arrogant disregard for the electorate. At this point we have to throw them out, give them a few years in the wilderness to lick their wounds and do a bit of thinking, and start to readjust their ideas. After a while, they'll become an electable alternative to the bunch we've got at present. It happens again and again. I hope Starmer & Co have just about reached that stage, because I'm afraid Rishi's bunch are pretty rapidly approaching their Use By date. And I really, really hope that by the time the incoming Labour government has run its course, the Conservative Party will have found a real leader again, and given itself a serious talking-to!
