Question: Are countries like companies? They don’t have the capacity to take everyone who wants to live there/offer a job to everyone? Will there always be winners & losers in immigration, with also good applicants declined & unsuitable ones that get through?
Answer: Well, yes. As a question, this reminds me of a line from Basil in Fawlty Towers: “Sybil Fawlty: specialist subject, The Bleedin’ Obvious”! No country, and no company, anywhere, can just accept anyone and everyone - not if it plans, or even vaguely hopes, to remain half-way viable. Put it at an even simpler, smaller, more domestic level - a household. You probably quite like the house, or the apartment or whatever, that you currently live in. It might even be the nicest in your street, and everyone in a less-nice place in your street would really like to live there. Maybe you feel a bit mean for having this desirable residence, and thereby denying it to everyone else. So fling the doors open! Put up a sign inviting anyone and everyone to come and live there too, and share in your undeserved good fortune. You can stop feeling selfish and guilty now - it's free to all. But how long will it remain a nice place to live? It'll quickly become badly overcrowded. Fights will break out as an inevitable result, and the place will become dirty and poorly maintained when no-one wants to share the housework, especially tidying up after strangers they don't know and don't understand or like. It will gradually turn from a lovely house into a squalid slum. In the end, you might even feel forced to give up, get out, and find somewhere less crowded, even though it's less nice than your house, or than it used to be. André, you seem to have a fixed belief that everyone should have an absolute right to live absolutely anywhere. In an ideal world, possibly. But we live in a world whose population has quadrupled in my lifetime, and no country anywhere could accommodate 8 billion people and retain any semblance of its original self. And the very characteristics that made it an attractive destination in the first place will simply disappear. It cannot work!

You would need to go to the UCAS website (ucas.com) and search for suitable courses at assorted universities, and then contact them individually, and discuss the make-up of their courses, their usual entry requirements, your own qualifications, and how far your combination of experience and qualifications would fit you for study on their course. Question: What happens if we get caught doing plagiarism in IGCSE?
Answer: What would you expect? It's dishonesty, it's cheating, it's theft of intellectual property, it's fraudulent. At the very least you'll be disqualified from that exam, and quite possibly from others in the same series. I first came across this problem about 25 years ago, when most teachers had barely heard of the Internet, and had very little idea of what was possible. GCSE in those days allowed up to 100% coursework in some subjects (not any longer, of course) and two of my GCSE English retakers submitted identical essays as their final bits of coursework, for the Shakespeare element. I couldn't prove where the work had come from, but clearly not from either of them. The vocabulary was too good, for one thing, and in any case their essay didn't quite answer the question in the title - almost certainly it was one they had downloaded, one with a similar title. My Head of Department backed me, despite lots of blustering on the part of the students, and threats of legal action from their parents, and refused to accept the work. Their folders of work were submitted with no Shakespeare essays, and they both failed as a result. This meant they couldn't go on to do A levels with us, and had to leave the College. A few years later, a Hong Kong student produced work in a practice test for IELTS that was clearly way better than he could do. It was made up of extracts from at least 3 different websites - and he'd done this under test conditions! We couldn't prove how he'd done it, though we were fairly sure, and he flatly denied cheating - but when he was caught cheating in the real IELTS test some weeks later, he was not only disqualified from that exam, but also barred from re-entering it in the future. I'm sure you think you're too clever to be caught, but so did these students, and they all came badly unstuck. It really is not worth the risk. Don't even try it!

Question: I'm a UK citizen living in the UK and attend college full time. Is it true that I'm not allowed to work more than 20 hours a week?

Question: The Met Police stopped a man for looking "openly Jewish" on a Saturday while the bi-weekly anti-Jew march was on. How can anyone deny London is a no-go zone for Jewish people every other Saturday?
Answer: Firstly, let me declare my open position as being one of huge sympathy for the Jewish people, in the UK, in Israel and around the world. Most Christians I know feel much the same. That said, I also have a certain sympathy for the police officer in this incident. When policing public events, their No. 1 job is to prevent any Breach of the Peace, and I'm pretty sure that would have been his aim in this case. Had things been less heated and pressing, my guess is that he would probably have said something like this: “Look, sir, the way you are dressed says pretty plainly that you're Jewish. Frankly, in the present company, that's brave, but asking for trouble; some people might call it provocative. You're free to dress as you choose, just as you're free to express your faith, but right here, it's not a good idea. It's my job to keep blood off the streets, so if you don't mind, sir, could you please take a different route?” Unfortunately, he didn't have the time that I've had to phrase it diplomatically, and expressed himself carelessly. I'll bet he has been kicking himself for this, ever since the words left his mouth. London is not a no-go area for anyone, but there are times and places where it's not sensible to be. It's quite wrong that this should be so, but it is. So please can we avoid jumping to extreme conclusions, and hurling accusations around? Edit, a few days later: The more that surfaces about this story, the more I stand by my answer. It seems that Gideon Falter approached a cordoned-off area, blocked off by the police, accompanied by a cameraman and a “security team” of 25, and tried to force his way through the police lines. He was not being so much “openly Jewish” as “ostentatiously Jewish.” He was very clearly looking for confrontation - and the police were doing their job in trying to prevent just such conflict. This isn't racism or antisemitism. This is the police doing just the same as they would with opposing squads of any description, such as football supporters - keeping the peace. End of!
